ops.title: De-faking trades stale modeled bytes for environment dependence — budget for CI-only failures
ops.body:
Replacing PATH shell fakes with real tools removes the fake-lie failure mode
(hand-modeled bytes drifting from what the tool emits) and **installs a
different one in its place**: the real tool's behavior now varies with the
environment, and the CI environment is not the dev machine.

Measured 2026-08-03, converting cc-context's vcs suite. The local suite was
green three times in a row; CI then went red twice, both times on a test no
local run could have failed:

1. **`TestVcsInfoWithoutGh`** — asserted gh was absent. Locally gh is in
   `/opt/homebrew/bin`, which the fixture's brew-free PATH excludes; on CI it is
   `/usr/bin/gh`, which that PATH deliberately KEEPS. See the sibling note on
   brew-free PATH and absence.
2. **`TestShimDepthSeparatesGTChildren`** — asserted the exact multiset of git
   calls `gt state` spawns. gt's DETACHED CACHE REFRESHER re-runs an
   environment-dependent subset of its probes; a warm dev machine produced 11
   rows, CI produced 9. The test's own comment said "measured stable at 11
   across repeated quiesced runs" — stable on one machine.

Both are the same shape: **a real tool's incidental behavior pinned as if it
were the contract.**

The rule that falls out: when a test converts onto real tools, assert the
PROPERTY under test, not the tool's full observable output.
- Depth separation is the claim; the exact spawn multiset is gt's business.
  Assert depth-0 is exactly the direct call, depth-1 is non-empty and all-git,
  and the settled probes are PRESENT — admit repeats.
- Tool absence is the claim; the brew-free PATH is not a mechanism for it.

Corollary for planning: budget for one or two CI-only rounds after a large
de-faking change. A green local suite is weaker evidence than it was before the
conversion, because the fixtures now depend on what is installed and how it
behaves, not just on what someone typed. Neither failure was a regression in
ccx; both were tests over-specifying a third party.
